basis.saw: the journal's globe emblem; byte-identical (sha256 08911ebd…) on all 13 pages, so one look covers every copy

narrative.text: The journal's publisher mark: a stylised blue globe encircled by the title of the Journal of International Social Research in Turkish and English. Page furniture, repeated once on every page; it carries no content of the article.

basis.saw: a solid black horizontal bar, 647 bytes, with no text, rule or structure in it

narrative.text: A solid black horizontal bar. A rendering artefact of the page layout; it carries no information.

basis.saw: a block diagram headed 'SWOT Analysis' splitting into Internal and External Factors

narrative.text: Block diagram decomposing SWOT: a single 'SWOT Analysis' box divides into 'Internal Factors — Strengths, Weaknesses' and 'External Factors — Opportunities, Threats'. This is the axis the method turns on: the first two are attributes of the organisation, the second two of its environment.

basis.saw: a four-row table defining Organizational Strengths, Organizational Weaknesses, Environmental Opportunities and Environmental Threats

narrative.text: Four-row definition table. Organizational Strengths: characteristics that give advantage over others in the industry. Organizational Weaknesses: characteristics that place the organisation at a disadvantage relative to others. Environmental Opportunities: external elements that give benefits for the organization. Environmental Threats: external elements that could cause trouble for it.

basis.saw: a two-part checklist table: 'Possible Organizational Strengths and Weaknesses' over four columns, then 'Sources of Possible Environmental Opportunities and Threats'

narrative.text: Checklist table in two parts. The first lists candidate internal factors in four columns — among them advertising, brand names, channel management, company reputation, costs, customer loyalty, distribution, economies of scale, financial resources, human resources, leadership, management, market share, organizational structure, product/service quality, purchasing, quality control, research and development, selling and technology. The second lists the sources of external factors: economic, political-legal, social, technological and industry forces.

basis.saw: a two-column checklist of internal factors grouped under seven numbered business functions

narrative.text: Internal-factor checklist grouped by business function: 1. Marketing (product quality, number of product lines, product differentiation, market share, pricing policies, distribution channels, promotional programs, customer service, marketing research, advertising, sales force); 2. Research and Development; 3. Management Information System; 4. Management Team; 5. Operations; 6. Finance; 7. Human Resources. It is the internal half of the scan, organised by where in the organisation to look.

basis.saw: a six-part list of external change categories, each item paired with what it impacts

narrative.text: External-factor checklist in six categories, each item stating what it impacts: 1. Societal changes (customer preferences, population trends); 2. Governmental changes (new legislation, new enforcement priorities); 3. Economic changes (interest rates, exchange rates, real personal income); 4. Competitive changes (new technologies, new competitors, price changes, new products); 5. Supplier changes (input cost, supply, number of suppliers); 6. Market changes (new uses of product, new market, product obsolescence). The external counterpart to the internal checklist.

basis.saw: a four-quadrant SWOT matrix filled in for a sportswear brand, quadrants labelled Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats

narrative.text: The paper's worked example: a completed four-quadrant SWOT matrix for an international sportswear brand (Nike). Strengths include global brand recognition, reputation for quality, a lean contract-manufacturing model, R&D, Fortune 500 standing and innovative marketing. Weaknesses include income dependence on footwear, retail price sensitivity, past non-disclosure about partner companies, and labour-practice allegations. Opportunities include fashion-driven replacement demand, product extension into sportswear, sunglasses and jewellery, and emerging markets. Threats include currency exposure, a highly competitive market, price-comparison behaviour and environmental/recession pressure.

basis.saw: a two-cell table fragment continuing the previous matrix — a Nike Technology opportunity on the left and the tail of the threats cell on the right

narrative.text: Overflow fragment of the worked SWOT matrix on the preceding page, carrying the last opportunity (Nike Technology, a footwear sensor interacting with Apple's iPod to record distance run and calories burned) and the tail of the threats cell (adverse publicity from widespread advertising).

basis.saw: a 2x2 matrix crossing Strengths and Weaknesses against Opportunities and Threats, each cell naming a strategy

narrative.text: The TOWS matrix: strengths and weaknesses across the top, opportunities and threats down the side, each cell naming the strategy that pairing implies. SO — achieve opportunities that greatly match the organization's strengths. WO — overcome weaknesses to attain opportunities. ST — use strengths to reduce vulnerability to threats. WT — prevent weaknesses to avoid making the organization more susceptible to threats. This is the step that turns the four lists into strategy.
